thesis.claim: The baseline stops improving within a few hundred iterations. Played against the brains of their own world's iteration 300, the brains of iteration 1,000 hold between 45% and 55% of a contested world: no better and no worse. The brains of iteration 300 have learned something all the same: against the founders' brains they hold more than 60%.
thesis.why: A world whose statistics have settled may be finished, or may be running in place — every lineage changing, none getting ahead, as in a Red Queen race. Nothing measured inside one moment tells the two apart; playing the brains of two moments against each other does (Cliff and Miller 1995). A pilot of the same world (seed 1, 5,000 tokens, eras every 100 iterations to 600, two contests per pair): against the founders, the brains of iteration 100 held 74% and those of iterations 200 to 600 held 77–90%; every pair of eras from iteration 200 on scored between 45% and 59% (median 50%). As Elo ratings against the founders: +283 at iteration 100, then +320 to +345 to iteration 600.
thesis.confirm: Over the ten worlds, the median world's score of the brains of iteration 1,000 against those of iteration 300 — the mean of its two contests, one in each era's world — lies between 0.45 and 0.55, and the median world's score of the brains of iteration 300 against the founders' is above 0.6.
thesis.refute: The median world's score of iteration 1,000 against iteration 300 is above 0.55: the baseline keeps improving. Or the score of iteration 300 against the founders is 0.6 or less: there was nothing to learn, or it was not learned.
